- **Audio-first: karaoke read-aloud and a reliable audio unlock** (verified; https://apps.apple.com/us/app/learn-to-read-duolingo-abc/id1440502568 and https://www.nngroup.com/articles/kids-cognition/) — Duolingo ABC's listing says stories read words aloud and highlight each word as it is spoken (App Store copy, company claim). NN/g reports that audio can fail silently: on one app, browser blocking meant participants never heard the explanation. The same Duolingo ABC listing has a parent review asking for an option to reduce the sound effects for correct answers. _Why:_ For a child who reads slowly and with effort, word-level highlighting links sound and text, so the narration also trains reading rather than only replacing it. Browser autoplay policy is a real risk for a web/PWA product. _For Davlatjon:_ Today the 'Прочитать' button on a task (fresh-phone-day1-t1-t1.jpg) plays recorded narration but offers no text tracking. Use ElevenLabs' character-level timestamps (background knowledge: the text-to-speech 'with timestamps' endpoint) at build time to store a small timing JSON per clip, then highlight the current word. For every task, auto-play the question once after the first user tap on the page (to satisfy autoplay rules) with a visible speaker button as a fallback and a clear 'tap to hear' state if audio is blocked. Add a 'quiet mode' (effects off, narration on) and a volume slider in the child's settings.
- **A good toy needs no instructions (play first, explain in context)** (verified; https://www.killscreen.com/what-designers-can-learn-about-play-children/) — The Kill Screen piece describes Toca Boca's approach: open-ended play with no imposed goals ('I had no goals or rules to follow'), 'A good toy doesn't need instructions' (designer Willow Mellbratt), and watching children as experts in play. Games, by contrast, emphasise a pre-defined set of rules and objectives with a right and wrong way to play. NN/g notes the opposite for tasks with a goal: Starfall's counting game with no stated goal confused children, so state the goal explicitly. _Why:_ Exploration lowers pressure; clear goals reduce confusion. Both are true: toys for free play, tasks for learning, each labelled honestly. _For Davlatjon:_ Separate the two modes visibly. 'Tasks' state the goal with an icon plus audio in one sentence ('Make the scale level'). 'Lab' (a sandbox) opens the same interactive tools (robot programmer, balance scales, number machines, Hanoi, river crossing, ciphers) with no score, no hints counter and no 'check' button; the object just responds. The daily quest can include one 'play in the Lab for 2 minutes' item. For chess, a free board where pieces can be moved without a rules engine complaint, and a 'show me where it can go' tap.
- **Competition that is optional, similar-level and kind to losers** (verified; https://blog.duolingo.com/duolingo-leagues-leaderboards/ and https://kahoot.com/blog/2025/07/17/kahoot-impact-research-academic-stress/) — Duolingo leagues: 10 leagues, a new weekly league each Sunday, learners matched with others of similar study habits and time zone; leaderboards are optional (turn off via profile visibility); Duolingo says only that testing in 2018 found 'a little competition worked for a lot of learners' and gives no outcome data. Kahoot's own blog says timers and public scoreboards can cause stress for some students and recommends options to turn them off; the research it cites is on university students (a 2024 study with 176 students and a 2025 meta-analysis of 43 studies) and is company-framed, with no breakdown by age or by timer/leaderboard. _Why:_ Matching by level keeps the odds fair; opt-out and no public shaming keep it safe. Evidence for children aged 6-12 specifically is thin; do not assume the adult results carry over. _For Davlatjon:_ For Dilnoza: 'beat your last week' personal-best cards, a weekly 'challenge a friend' on the same set of 5 puzzles shared by a link or QR (no accounts, no global ranking), and printable rank certificates that already exist (a good brag artifact). Show results as 'you both solved it' or time-free scores. No timers by default on tasks (Woodpecker and Storm modes keep their timer but with a clearly marked 'timed' label and an exit that is never penalised). Keep the owner's rule: no rating numbers shown to children under 10.
- **No lives: let the hint ladder be the only 'resource'** (unverified; Duolingo hearts-to-energy change, third-party summaries seen in search (not opened: unanswered.io, lingoly.io and others). Quote attributed to Duolingo: 'Hearts: each mistake cost 1 heart for free learners. This was especially frustrating for beginners.') — Duolingo is reported to have replaced hearts with an 'energy' meter (rollout reported in 2025; sources disagree on dates) so the system rewards correct answers rather than penalising mistakes; free learners still lose energy on mistakes and subscribers have it unlimited. Reception is reported as mixed. _Why:_ The lesson is the stated rationale: penalty-for-mistakes systems are especially discouraging for beginners. I could not verify these details first-hand. _For Davlatjon:_ Keep what the owner already has: hints open one by one, no 'wrong'. Do not add hearts, energy or a daily cap on tasks. If a limit is wanted for wellbeing, make it a friendly, parent-set 'rest time' at the end of a round (see the session pattern) and never sell it.
- **Round-based sessions with a natural stop and pause/save** (verified; https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/childrens-information/childrens-code-guidance-and-resources/age-appropriate-design-a-code-of-practice-for-online-services/13-nudge-techniques/) — The ICO Children's Code nudge standard (opened): for ages 0-12, 'Nudge towards wellbeing enhancing behaviours (such as taking breaks)', and for all ages 'Provide tools to support wellbeing enhancing behaviours (such as mid-level pause and save features)'. The page does not name reward loops or streaks (the draft coverage that did is secondary). Toca Boca reviewers (Screenwise, not opened) argue that no timers or game-over screens make leaving the tablet easier; that is a reviewer's interpretation, not a company statement. _Why:_ Short, finishable units match about 10 minutes of attention. The ICO text is also a legal-style signal that building breaks in is expected of children's services. _For Davlatjon:_ kid7-phone-home-t1.jpg promises 'Неделя 1 · День 1... 8 задач · около 25 минут'. For a 7-year-old this is the wrong unit. Split a day into 3 rounds of 2-3 tasks (about 6-8 minutes) with a 'Round complete' screen, a stop button as large as 'Next', and auto-save of the current task. After round 1 or 2 offer 'Take a break - Robot will wait' as the primary button, with 'Another round' as the secondary. Change the home card to '1 round - 7 minutes'. For the parent add a soft 'session suggestion' (not a lock) in /parent.
- **Unexpected, informative rewards and collections that celebrate thinking** (unverified; Lingokids reward system per its help centre, seen in search results only (page returned 403 on open): one star per different activity, 5 stars unlock a sticker pack, stickers go into an album and a scene book. Overjustification: Lepper, Greene and Nisbett 1973 (J. Personality and Social Psychology, doi 10.1037/h0035519), abstract seen via search, not opened.) — Lingokids ties stars to distinct activities (replaying does not add a star), so the collection rewards breadth. The classic overjustification study found preschoolers promised a 'good player' ribbon for drawing later played less with the pens than unrewarded or unexpectedly rewarded children. A 1995 meta-analysis found the effect holds in the conditions it predicts and not for non-contingent or unexpected rewards. Deci, Koestner and Ryan 1999 is the usual counter-citation; I did not verify it. The effect is contested in size and conditions, not a universal law. _Why:_ Rewards that recognise variety and effort and arrive unexpectedly are less likely to turn an interesting puzzle into a chore. _For Davlatjon:_ The existing 'Мои привычки мыслителя' (habits) card is the right idea. Make stickers or robot parts come from process behaviours: 'tried a different way', 'opened a hint and then solved it', 'explained why', 'tried a new tool'. Do not reward speed or streak length. Show one surprise sticker at the end of some rounds (announced as 'a gift from the robot') rather than a promise before the task. Keep crowns for robot wins but do not require them to progress.
- **Language-neutral, short onboarding for RU/UZ with the voice as the guide** (verified; https://www.nngroup.com/articles/kids-cognition/ and https://www.nngroup.com/articles/childrens-websites-usability-issues/) — NN/g: give clear, specific instructions that state the goal; visuals should carry meaning even without audio; subtle verbal cues fail across cultures (a 6-year-old in China did not understand 'Hooo'); children expect tappable characters and pictures and tend to poke around rather than follow a main path; redundant navigation is 'very confusing' for children; recommended font sizes 14 pt for young children and 12 for older. _Why:_ The same screen must work for a child who cannot yet read the sentence and for one who can; it must also survive translation into Uzbek. _For Davlatjon:_ audit-metrics shows 63 text nodes at 12 px on phone home and 16 at 10 px on /chess (minFs), small for a 7-year-old. Raise body and label text to at least 14-16 px for the 6-8 mode, and make 'bigText' effectively the default there. Use icon + one-line label + speaker for every main card on the home screen, and merge duplicate paths (home has several routes to chess and tasks; the chess page has 48 interactive elements and 8 phone tiles, kid7-phone-chess-t1..t8) into one 'Today' path. Make every section tile tappable with an illustration, with a 'Parents' lock tucked away from the child's main nav.
- **No guilt notifications; parent-addressed, opt-in reminders only** (unverified; https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/childrens-information/childrens-code-guidance-and-resources/age-appropriate-design-a-code-of-practice-for-online-services/13-nudge-techniques/ (verified for the ICO text); Duolingo notification claims from Taplytics/Ngrow/Boykis summaries seen in search, not opened.) — Duolingo's notification system is reported to use multi-armed bandits to choose messages, with a +0.5% DAU and +2% new-user retention gain in a paper cited by a newsletter, and a tone that ranges from encouraging to guilt-tripping (all third-party, unverified). The ICO text I opened says not to use nudge techniques to get children to give unnecessary personal data and 'You should not exploit unconscious psychological processes to this end'; it names human affirmation needs as an example. That standard is about data and privacy, so I do not claim it bans reminders in general. _Why:_ The measured lift is small and the mascot-guilt tone is the most criticised part of Duolingo's design. For a 6-12 audience the decision-maker for 'should my child study today' is the parent. _For Davlatjon:_ As a PWA do not ask the child for notification permission. In /parent offer an opt-in weekly summary (Telegram message is a natural channel in Uzbekistan) written to the parent: 'This week: 3 rounds, a new skill: balance scales', with a one-tap 'share with the teacher'. If a daily reminder exists, it is set by the parent at a time they choose, with neutral copy and no sad robot, no countdown and no streak threat.

Anti-patterns:

- Loss-framed streaks with paid repair and a '0' after a gap — Duolingo's own post says motivation shifts to loss aversion as streaks grow and that losing one can be demotivating; a third-party guide lists paid or plan-based repair. For children, who have weaker executive function (NN/g), this creates a daily obligation and anxiety; the ICO draft coverage lists streaks among reward loops it worries about (secondary source). Use weekly dots, free rest days and 'welcome back'.
- Hearts / energy lives that stop learning after mistakes — Duolingo itself said hearts were 'especially frustrating for beginners' (as reported, not first-hand). Penalising errors teaches a 7-year-old to avoid trying. Davlatjon's soft feedback and free hint ladder are the better model.
- Guilt-tripping mascot and notifications ('Don't let Duo down') — Reported in third-party commentary as 'guilt marketing'; for children it turns a friendly character into a source of shame. Davlatjon's robot should never express disappointment; reminders go to parents only.
- Public leaderboards, ranks and visible rating numbers for kids — Kahoot's own blog says public scoreboards and timers can cause stress for some students; evidence for primary-age children is thin. The owner's rule of no rating numbers under 10 is correct and should extend to any peer ranking.
- Cancellation traps, negative-option trials and hidden billing — The FTC case against ABCmouse (complaint 2 Sept 2020, $10 million, refunds of $9.7 million announced 19 April 2021, opened on ftc.gov) alleged misrepresented cancellation terms and charges without proper consent; the company disputed the broad allegations. Any future paid plan in Davlatjon needs a plain-language, one-step cancel and no child-facing purchase prompts.
- Variable-reward mystery boxes, ad-watch bonuses and characters that beg for purchases — The UOW/Deakin article (opened) lists variable rewards as especially effective, double rewards for watching ads and characters urging purchases, citing studies without detail, and gives an unpublished anecdote of a 12-year-old spending several hundred dollars on a Genshin Impact character. NN/g (opened) found children cannot tell ads from real content. Keep Davlatjon ad-free and rewards non-random and non-purchasable.
- Timers and countdowns on learning tasks for 6-8 — Time pressure conflicts with the 'think, do not rush' principle shown on the welcome screen and with slow readers like Aziz; Kahoot's own guidance is to allow turning timers off. Restrict timers to clearly marked, optional challenge modes.
- Endless autoplay of the next task with no exit — Autoplay is described in children's-design commentary as manipulative (as in the FTC dark-patterns staff report coverage, secondary) and the ICO asks for breaks and pause/save for under-13s. Use a 'Round complete' screen instead of auto-advance.
- Tiny 'X', parent lock and header icons for child-facing controls — NN/g saw 7-year-olds fail to hit a 5 mm button and land in an app store. Davlatjon header icons are 36x34 and 42x34 CSS px (audit-metrics 'phone /'), well below the 2 cm (about 76 px) recommendation; mistaken taps on parent or external links break trust.
- Shaming opt-outs and cheerful 'wrong' sounds — Buttons like 'No, I don't want to learn' are confirmshaming (state attorneys' term, secondary). Khan Academy Kids' 'bong' for an incorrect answer is a good fit for their audience but would clash with Davlatjon's no-'wrong' tone; use a neutral, soft cue.

### Interactive math and logic platforms: what to adopt for children 6-12 in Davlatjon

Most vendor effectiveness claims in this space are weak. Prodigy says its own evidence is correlational (ESSA Tier 3). Zearn's independent RCT (RAND, Texas) found a non-significant effect on the state test and 0.11 SD on an exploratory adaptive test. A 2026 design-based study of DragonBox found mixed results: playful moments, but play did not reliably build algebra. So I rely on design principles I could open and read (Desmos' design guide, Brilliant's about page, Math Academy's method page, NN/g child-UX articles, the Sinha & Kapur productive-failure meta-analysis abstract, an arXiv hint-design study) and label everything else as unverified. Three findings matter most for 6-12. (1) Problem-solving-before-instruction (productive failure) helps overall (g=0.36) but the same meta-analysis found grades 2-5 favoured instruction-first, so Aziz needs a worked example or scaffold first, and only Dilnoza-age children should get open struggle. (2) Desmos argues immediate feedback can invite guess-and-check, so ask for a prediction first, then show an interpretive reaction to the child's own idea instead of a verdict. (3) NN/g recommends about 2cm x 2cm touch targets for young children and found that children skip long instructions. What the live app already does well: no 'wrong' wording ('Давай проверим твою идею!'), hints that open one at a time with a good intro line ('Сначала попробуй подумать сам'), a Run + Step robot tool, a checkmark strip of task icons, reflection chips ('Было трудно, но я справился'), a 'Прочитать' button, and a difficulty chip. Gaps seen in the screenshots and a live Playwright run: (a) task 1 (kid7-phone-day1-t1-t1.jpg) is a typed number plus 'Проверить', which reads as a test, not a puzzle; (b) the wrong-answer reply asks an abstract question ('Какая часть решения точно верная?') with no visual of the child's own steps; (c) instruction text is long for a 7-year-old (6 lines in rich-phone-day1-robot-t1.jpg, 6 lines in rich-phone-w2d3-t1.jpg), and the home card promises 8 tasks, about 25 minutes (kid7-phone-home-t1.jpg) against Aziz's roughly 10 minutes; (d) 11-14 targets under 44 px on task pages (audit-metrics.json) while NN/g suggests about 2cm (roughly 120 CSS px on a Pixel 7 by my arithmetic) for young children, so the 44 px floor is a minimum, not a goal. Disclosure: one of my Playwright screenshots (wrong.png) was briefly written into /home/user/Davlatjon because I used a relative path; I moved it to my scratchpad folder immediately and the repo has no leftover file from me.

- **Predict first, then reveal (delay the verdict)** (verified; https://blog.desmos.com/articles/the-desmos-guide-to-building-great-digital-math/) — Desmos's design guide says to 'ask for estimations before calculations', to create an intellectual need before teaching a skill, and warns that immediate feedback can invite guess-and-check instead of thinking; it recommends delaying feedback so students predict first. The same guide says to ask for informal reasoning (sketches, guesses) before formal analysis. _Why:_ The child commits to an idea, so the reveal is a surprise to explain rather than a grade to fear. It also turns a drill into a small mystery. It is a practitioner design guide, not a controlled study. _For Davlatjon:_ In tasks like 'Почти двадцать: 19+19+19' (kid7-phone-day1-t1-t1.jpg), show three big picture chips first ('ближе к 40 / 50 / 60?') with audio, lock in the guess, then open the keypad or manipulative. After the answer, show the child's guess next to the true value ('Ты думал 50, получилось 57. Почти!'). Do it for numeric, scale and number-machine tasks; skip it in speed drills and in chess tactics where the prediction is the move itself.
- **Interpretive feedback that replays the child's own idea** (verified; https://blog.desmos.com/articles/the-desmos-guide-to-building-great-digital-math/) — Desmos: give students chances to be right and wrong 'in different, interesting ways' and treat interesting wrong answers as formative assessment; keep expository screens short and connect feedback to the student's existing thinking. Brilliant's about page (https://brilliant.org/about/) also says each interactive problem gives instant, custom feedback based on your answer and that its tutor 'asks instead of tells'. NN/g (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/childrens-websites-usability-issues/) found children 'struggled to interpret error messages'. _Why:_ Text like 'try again' gives a 7-year-old nothing to act on. Showing what their answer would imply lets them find the slip themselves and keeps the soft tone. _For Davlatjon:_ I submitted 50 for 19+19+19 in the live app (scratchpad .../audit-agents/interactive/wrong.png). The reply was a soft card: 'Давай проверим твою идею! Какая часть решения точно верная?'. That wording is good (no 'wrong'), but it asks an abstract question and shows nothing. For age under 10, have the robot mascot replay the child's number visually (three groups of 19 as blocks, then 19+19=38 highlighted) and ask a concrete question with 2 big tap choices ('38 или 40?'). Add 2-3 'common slip' replies per task, authored from likely wrong answers (e.g. 50 = 20+20+10).
- **Direct manipulation with tap alternatives and big targets** (verified; https://www.nngroup.com/articles/children-ux-physical-development/) — NN/g: ages 6-8 have limited fine motor skills; dragging, scrolling and tapping small objects are hard on desktop, while tapping, swiping and dragging suit touchscreens because they use big arm and hand movements; they recommend at least 2cm x 2cm touch targets for young children; from about 9 more advanced interaction becomes possible; around 11 children match adults physically. _Why:_ Manipulatives (balance scales, number machines, Hanoi) beat typed answers for engagement, but only if the target is large enough to hit. Everything is solvable by tapping, with drag as an optional shortcut. (Carbonneau et al. 2013, a meta-analysis of manipulatives, reports small-to-moderate benefits; I did not open its full text, so I do not rely on its effect sizes.) _For Davlatjon:_ Replace the typed '?' box on warm-up tasks with a manipulative where possible (ten-frames, tap-to-add blocks, a number line with a draggable pin). Provide tap-to-select then tap-to-place for Hanoi and balance scales. The measured numbers show the gap: task pages have 11-14 targets under 44 px (audit-metrics.json: 'phone /week/1/day/1' small44=11, '#task-5' small44=14). Make the primary answer controls 64-96 CSS px for age under 9 (NN/g's 2cm is about 120 CSS px on a Pixel 7 by my arithmetic) and keep the 44 px floor for secondary controls. The robot arrow keys (about 48 CSS px in rich-phone-day1-robot-t2.jpg) are fine as a floor but could be larger for Aziz.
- **Concreteness fading (picture, then symbol)** (unverified; background knowledge (Fyfe, McNeil, Son & Goldstone 2014, Educational Psychology Review 26:9-25; I confirmed the title and year via Semantic Scholar but could not open the abstract)) — Start with a concrete, manipulable representation, then explicitly and gradually replace it with more abstract ones (picture, then dots, then symbols). The authors describe it as a systematic review recommendation, not a meta-analysis; a later paper (Kokkonen & Schalk) suggests it may not generalise as widely as claimed. DragonBox uses a similar move by replacing cards with numbers and variables over time (publisher's own account, not independently verified). _Why:_ Symbols are interpreted through objects the child already understands. The fade has to be explicit and gradual, or the child learns the object game and not the maths. _For Davlatjon:_ For number machines and balance scales, run each concept in 3 steps over several days: blocks you can move, then the same layout with numerals on the blocks, then a plain equation. Show the previous step as a small ghost image next to the new one so the link is visible. Tag each task with its fade stage so the day plan can step up only after 2 successes.
- **Hint ladder where the last rung is a partly worked step in the workspace** (verified; https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371) — An arXiv study of an intelligent tutor compared 'Assertions' (partially worked example steps placed in the student's own workspace) with text 'Messages' shown after inactivity. Assertions significantly increased unsolicited hint use, and children with low prior proficiency produced shorter, more efficient posttest solutions, faster. A 2020 hint-factory paper (via search results, not opened) makes a similar point: partially worked hints require work and reduce 'clicking through' to the answer. _Why:_ Children who need help often do not ask for it; a hint that appears as a step on the board is read and used, and it still leaves a gap to fill. _For Davlatjon:_ The app's ladder already opens one by one with a good intro ('Застрял? Подсказки открываются по одной. Сначала попробуй подумать сам — это самое интересное!' in rich-phone-day1-t1-t2.jpg, 5 dots). Keep it. Change the content of rungs 3-5 so they act on the board (the robot tool draws the first 2 arrows greyed out; the balance tool pre-places one weight) instead of describing it in text. Use the existing 'hint pause' setting as the rate limiter (kid7 scenario). Show a small 'hint used' dot per rung on the task strip, not a penalty.
- **Age-calibrated struggle: scaffold first for under 10, try-first for 11-12** (verified; https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.3102/00346543211019105?fields=title,year,abstract) — Sinha & Kapur 2021 (Review of Educational Research) meta-analysed 53 studies, 166 comparisons: problem-solving before instruction (PS-I) beat instruction-first with a moderate effect (Hedges g = 0.36), larger (0.37-0.58) when the design followed Productive Failure principles. But younger learners (grades 2-5) and domain-general skills showed the opposite pattern, favouring instruction first. A press summary (Education Today, opened) says the approach suits secondary and undergraduate students better than primary students and that the studies centre on STEM concepts. _Why:_ Younger children often lack the prior knowledge to generate useful attempts, so unaided struggle just produces frustration. Older children benefit from exploring first. _For Davlatjon:_ Use the existing age setting (settings.age) to choose the task opening. Age 6-9: a 15-second worked demo, then one guided attempt, then free. Age 10-12: show the puzzle first, let them try for a minute, then offer the 'show me a method' button. The current app opens with the task and a text line ('Сначала посчитай так, как тебе удобно...'), which is the try-first pattern for everyone. That is good for Dilnoza and risky for Aziz. Label the difficulty chip ('Комфортно') as the app already does, and let the chip adapt to the observed success.
- **Worked example first, then fade the support** (verified; https://www.mathacademy.com/how-it-works) — Math Academy states that 'every knowledge point starts with a fully worked out example for students to follow along with' (it names the worked-example effect), gives only 'the necessary doses of information right before they use it', and advances only after demonstrated mastery. It also runs an adaptive diagnostic placement and spaced repetition. The page is the vendor's own description, not outside evidence, and the product targets older learners. _Why:_ New tools (balance scales, number machines, ciphers) cost working memory. Seeing one done first leaves capacity for the idea itself. _For Davlatjon:_ Day intro screens like 'Начни с малого' (rich-phone-w2d3-t1.jpg) are a 6-line paragraph plus a 'habit of the day' chip. For ages 6-9 replace the paragraph with a 20-second animated example with the narration already available, then a half-done task (the child finishes the last step), then a solo task. Keep the habit chip: it is a good, short idea.
- **Short, finishable sessions with a visible end** (verified; https://www.mathacademy.com/how-it-works) — Math Academy's 'necessary doses' idea plus its XP, which it ties to roughly one minute of focused effort per point. For young children, Mathseeds (background knowledge, unverified) schedules about 15-minute sessions. _Why:_ A child who can see the finish line starts more willingly and stops on a high note; the parent sees a short, safe session. _For Davlatjon:_ The home card for day 1 says '8 задач · около 25 минут' (kid7-phone-home-t1.jpg). Aziz's attention is about 10 minutes. Offer 'Мини-занятие: 3 задачи, 8 минут' as the default for age under 9, with the other 5 tasks as a 'бонус' after a celebration screen, and a 'на сегодня хватит' exit that still counts for the daily quest. The icon strip across the top (8 tasks with green checks) is an excellent progress device already.
- **Vary the verb and make it a problem to solve, not a form to fill** (verified; https://blog.desmos.com/articles/the-desmos-guide-to-building-great-digital-math/) — Desmos: 'An activity becomes tedious if students do the same kind of verb over and over again' (mix arguing, predicting, comparing with calculating); 'a problematic activity feels focused while a problem-free activity meanders'; make activities 'easy to start and difficult to finish'; create cognitive conflict by asking for a prediction and then showing a surprise. _Why:_ What separates a puzzle from a test is a visible goal, a world that responds, and no score attached. A typed answer into a box with a 'Проверить' button is the shape of a test. _For Davlatjon:_ Audit the day strip: in kid7-phone-day1-t1-t1.jpg the first two icons are the same warm-up type with a typed answer. Rotate verbs across a day: predict, build (robot, scales), sort/odd-one-out, spot-the-slip, explain to a parent (already present as the 'Объясни маме или папе' prompt, which is good). Give every task a visible goal state (robot to the flag, scale balanced, machine output matches the target) that lights up on success and let tries be free. Add one optional 'звёздочка' extension per task for Dilnoza (easy to start, hard to finish).
- **Progress as a journey and as effort, not just as a score** (verified; https://www.mathacademy.com/how-it-works) — Math Academy ties XP to effort (about a minute of focus per point) and builds a knowledge graph that updates after each task. Mathseeds (background knowledge, not opened) uses geographic 'maps' and hatching pets as rewards at the end of each lesson. Both make progress concrete: a place you are going to and something you grow. _Why:_ Children read a map and a growing creature faster than a number. Effort-based XP rewards trying, not only winning. _For Davlatjon:_ Build a week map (3 weeks x 7 days as islands or stations) on the home screen to replace or sit above the slogan hero ('Математика — это место, где происходят интересные вещи' wraps to 5 lines in kid7-phone-home-t1.jpg and tells a child nothing to do). Award XP for finishing, trying a hint ladder honestly and re-attempting, not only for first-try correctness. Dilnoza can screenshot a map or a certificate to show friends, which fits her need without public rankings.
- **Rewards tied to the work, no leaderboards or paywalled loot for children** (verified; https://fairplayforkids.org/pf/prodigy/) — A child-advocacy group (Fairplay) alleges that Prodigy shows paywalled treasure boxes, gives members cosmetic status ('kids without memberships literally walk in dirt'), uses social-comparison pop-ups, and congratulates children for shopping. Prodigy disputes the pressure claims (MediaPost summary of the 2021 FTC complaint). Separately, Hanus & Fox 2015 (Computers & Education) report that a gamified college course with leaderboard and badges showed lower motivation, satisfaction and exam scores than the non-gamified one; I confirmed the title and year via Semantic Scholar but did not open the abstract, and it is one study with adults. _Why:_ If the reward is a thing you made or a step you took (a robot program, a certificate, a creature that grows from effort), the child keeps the intrinsic goal. Rewards that depend on money or on comparison with others shift the goal. _For Davlatjon:_ Davlatjon's local-only progress and PIN-gated parent area already avoid most of this. Keep awards personal (certificates, crowns against the robot, personal bests). If a social element is wanted for Dilnoza, make it a shareable image of her own certificate, not a ranking. Never show other children's progress.
- **Praise the process and the strategy; not 'you are smart'** (unverified; background knowledge (Mueller & Dweck 1998, J. Personality and Social Psychology; I did not open the paper, only a secondary summary)) — In the 1998 studies with fifth graders, children praised for intelligence chose easier follow-up tasks and did worse after failure than children praised for effort. Later mindset work has replicated less strongly and with smaller effects, so the size of the effect is contested. _Why:_ Feedback about what the child did (a strategy, perseverance) keeps attention on the task, not on a verdict about themselves. _For Davlatjon:_ The 'Отметь, что получилось' chips are a good start ('Я нашёл другой способ', 'Было трудно, но я справился' in rich-phone-day1-t1-t2.jpg). Their Russian forms are masculine ('нашёл', 'справился'), which breaks the gender-neutral principle; rephrase with neutral forms ('Нашлось другое решение', 'Было трудно — получилось'). Celebration lines should name the action ('Ты проверил второй шаг — и нашёл ошибку!'), not the ability.
- **Short instructions: icon plus audio, text secondary** (verified; https://www.nngroup.com/articles/childrens-websites-usability-issues/) — NN/g (children 3-12): children skip long text, ignore long paragraphs of instructions, find redundant navigation 'very confusing', expect to tap and interact with pictures, and like animation and sound (unlike adults); reading ability ranges from none to tentative to scanning. The related NN/g physical-development article adds that for 7-9-year-olds 'clear instructions with images' work. _Why:_ Aziz reads slowly and with effort. The audio button helps only if it is found and used before the child gives up on the text. _For Davlatjon:_ The robot task intro is 6 lines of Russian text (rich-phone-day1-robot-t1.jpg) before the board appears; on a phone the board is below the fold. For age under 9: one-line instruction, a bigger 'Прочитать' button next to the title (it is about 50 CSS px tall now), optional auto-play of the narration the first time a task opens (tap-to-start to satisfy autoplay rules), and move the board above the text. Use icon-first rules ('стрелки -> флаг') with the text as a fallback. The measured home page has 63 text nodes under 14 px on /, 73 on /chess (audit-metrics.json); lift all child-facing text to at least 14-16 px.

Anti-patterns:

- Paywalled loot, status by payment, or ads inside the learning flow — Fairplay alleges (and Prodigy disputes) that Prodigy shows 16 membership ads against 4 math problems in 19 minutes, blocks free players from opening treasure boxes and gives members visible status; Common Sense Media parent reviews describe constant membership prompts. For children this turns learning into a request for money from parents. Davlatjon must keep the child flow free of any purchase surface.
- Nudges that exploit the need for approval, or streaks that punish absence — The UK ICO Children's Code standard on nudge techniques says not to use nudges that exploit unconscious psychological processes such as human affirmation needs, and encourages nudges toward wellbeing like taking breaks (I opened the page). The 2019 draft named streaks and likes as examples (from search results, not confirmed in the final text). Keep the gentle streak truly gentle: no loss messages, no guilt copy, no countdown, and a break reminder after the session.
- Leaderboards and public comparison for under-12s — Comparison shifts the goal from understanding to ranking; Hanus & Fox (single adult study, abstract not opened by me) found lower motivation with a leaderboard and badges, and Fairplay alleges Prodigy's social-comparison pop-ups pressure children. Dilnoza's wish to compete can be met with personal bests, a timed challenge against herself, and a certificate she shares by choice.
- Instant, free bottom-out hints (click-through to the answer) — Intelligent-tutor research on 'help abuse' (LearnLab wiki, unopened; secondary summary only) describes children clicking through the hint ladder to copy the answer, which weakens learning. Keep rungs one at a time with a short pause or an action between rungs; make the last rung a partly worked step, not the final answer.
- Guess-and-check loops with immediate right/wrong — Desmos warns that immediate feedback can invite guess-and-check instead of thinking. With a numeric keypad and an unlimited retry button, a child can try 10 numbers in 10 seconds. Add a prediction step or a brief 'explain it' beat before the verdict on key tasks.
- Praising ability ('ты умный') or using the word 'wrong' / red crosses — Mueller & Dweck 1998 (secondary summary only): ability praise made fifth graders avoid challenge; the effect size in later work is debated. The owner's rule against the word 'wrong' is sound; extend it to red crosses, buzzer sounds and loss animations.
- Game wrapper that is fun but does not build the maths — The 2026 DragonBox design-based study (Digital Experiences in Mathematics Education 12(2), opened) found playful moments and enjoyment, but play did not reliably develop algebraic knowledge; the authors needed 'wraparound' activities. Always add a short reflection or a transfer task ('how would you tell a friend?') after any game-like tool.
- Walls of text and abstract questions as feedback for readers under 9 — NN/g found children skip long instructions and struggle to interpret error messages. The current wrong-answer reply 'Какая часть решения точно верная?' is soft but abstract; a 6-line intro before the board (rich-phone-day1-robot-t1.jpg) makes Aziz quit before he starts.
- Speed pressure and timers on core tasks — Timers on primary tasks make slow readers like Aziz feel slow; keep timing only for optional, clearly labelled challenge modes (storm, Woodpecker) and never show a ranking against others. Background knowledge, not a source I opened.
- Endless 'next' with no natural stopping point — A day of 8 tasks at about 25 minutes (kid7-phone-home-t1.jpg) exceeds the attention window of a 7-year-old and the 'short, safe sessions' a parent wants. Provide a celebratory stopping point, and a break nudge, as the ICO page encourages.

### Chess learning platforms for children (ChessKid, Chess.com bots, Lichess, Chessable, Magnus Trainer, ChessKid Adventure) and what to adopt in Davlatjon's chess school

Davlatjon's chess school already has several things the best kids' platforms do. The board is full width on a 412 px phone with coordinates printed on the frame (kid7-phone-game-robot-t1.jpg). The five robots are characters with a speech bubble, and the robot picker has a "советуем тебе" badge. The tactics page has a "Мой уровень ⭐⭐" control with Полегче/По силам/Потруднее and no rating number (rich-phone-puzzles-t1.jpg). Drills are framed as "Пять минут в день" with a personal record (rich-phone-drills-t1.jpg). Lesson legends have a "Послушать" button. The research points to six gaps. (1) Make help a choice made before the game, and keep help from lowering rewards. (2) Make the first robot game winnable, and give each robot a recurring character and a personal record, not a rating. (3) Put the actions on the game screen where a thumb can reach them: in kid7-phone-game-robot-t1.jpg the Подсказка/Отменить row starts at about y=743 CSS px of an 839 px viewport, and the Перевернуть/Сдаться/Новая партия buttons are further down in t2. (4) Give Dilnoza a competitive mode that is unrated, has no public leaderboard and works on one device. (5) Keep every time-penalty mechanic away from the 6-8 age group. (6) Keep parent messaging about chess skill, not about "chess makes you smarter", because the strongest evidence says far transfer rarely occurs. Safety is the one area where the platforms agree: no free chat, auto-generated names, a guardian in the loop. That matters before Google/Telegram sync ships. Verification: items marked verified=true were opened and read. Chess Playground could not be fetched (DNS error), the Play Magnus claims come only from search snippets, and Common Sense Education's ChessKid review was no longer available, so none of those are cited as verified.

- **Bot ladder as recurring characters, with a recommended start and a personal record** (verified; https://www.chesskid.com/learn/articles/new-feature-bot-personalities and https://www.chesskid.com/learn/articles/chess-coaching-for-kids) — ChessKid names its bots after a recurring character (FunMasterMike at ages 6, 8, 10, 14, 18 and now), so difficulty is shown as an age ladder and not as a rating. The page says "I recommend starting with FunMasterMike at age 6 and working your way up". Kids can toggle coach mode and pick a colour, the bots speak during play, the app tracks your record against each bot ("How many can you beat?!"), and a win triggers confetti. Separate Pet Bots (Ziggy, Miss Pickels) are for first games, and six Zoo bots cover first steps to harder games. _Why:_ A character is easier for a child to remember than a number. A visible 'beaten / not yet' record is a personal goal with no peer comparison. A named starting point removes the choice problem for a 7-year-old. The description of how the bots work is only what the page states. I found no study on why it works, so that part is inference. _For Davlatjon:_ Keep the five piece-named robots, but give each a face, a recurring one-line voice clip and a pass mark ('Конь: побеждён ✓ / ещё нет'). Today the picker is a long vertical list of cards with chips (rich-phone-play-t1.jpg). Replace it with a horizontal path or a 5-step staircase of avatars, with a big 'Играть' button on the recommended one. The Pawn card says 'Ходит почти наугад' (a hard word for Aziz), so add an icon (a dice) and an audio clip. Persist 'beaten' per robot next to the crowns that already exist. Never show an Elo-like number.
- **First game must be winnable (gentle first bots)** (verified; https://www.chesskid.com/learn/articles/chess-coaching-for-kids (Pet Bots for first games and guiding beginners). The claim that Play Magnus's first level plays mostly at random is from a search snippet only.) — ChessKid describes Pet Bots (Ziggy and Miss Pickels) as made for first games and for guiding beginners, with six Zoo bots above them and Original Robots with 10 levels. The page does not say how the Pet Bots actually play. _Why:_ A first loss in the first minute is the strongest churn signal for a young beginner. A reachable first win gives early competence. This is general learning-psychology reasoning that I did not verify with a study. _For Davlatjon:_ The Pawn robot already 'moves almost at random but sometimes sees mate', which is right. Add a guaranteed-first-win guard: for a brand-new profile (no crowns), the Pawn robot never captures a protected piece and never ignores a mate-in-one for the child. Put 'Сыграй с Пешкой' as the one big button on the Play page for a first-time child, with the other four robots collapsed behind 'Другие роботы'. The 'Фора' chips (без ферзя, без ладьи, ...) are 32 px tall on the 412 px phone (measured by script) and are advanced; hide them for age under 10.
- **Help as a choice before the game, not as a button that costs you** (verified; https://support.chess.com/en/articles/8614091-how-can-i-play-against-the-chess-com-bots) — On Chess.com, bot games are always unrated. A mode picker (Challenge, Friendly, Assisted, Custom) decides how much help you get, and Custom lets you toggle hints, suggestion arrows, takebacks, evaluation bar and bot chat. Crowns are tied to the help used: no help 3 crowns, 1-3 hints or undos 2 crowns, 4 or more 1 crown. _Why:_ The child decides the amount of help before the stress starts, and an adult can see the setting. The crown tie is Chess.com's design for adults and teens, and I found no evidence it works for 6-8-year-olds. _For Davlatjon:_ Replace the in-game Подсказка / Отменить / Сдаться row with a three-icon choice on the robot picker: 'С помощником' (hint + undo on), 'Сам' (undo only), 'Турнир' (nothing). Default by age: 6-8 help on, 9-10 'Сам', 11-12 free choice. In kid7-phone-game-robot-t1.jpg the hint and undo row starts at about y=743 CSS px, right at the fold of the 839 px viewport, so Aziz has to scroll mid-game to find help. Once the mode is set, the in-game bar can shrink to one lightbulb. For crowns: keep one crown per win whatever the mode, and show a small gold or silver rim for 'without help' as a bonus, so asking for help never looks like losing something.
- **Adaptive bots that ease off after a blunder** (verified; https://support.chess.com/en/articles/8614091-how-can-i-play-against-the-chess-com-bots) — Chess.com's adaptive bot personalities change strength during the game. The article says they 'challenge you more if you're doing well and ease off if you make mistakes'. _Why:_ The child's performance in this game, not a guess from a rating, sets the pressure, so the game stays in a band where it is neither crushing nor boring. That is the design intent; I found no study of it with children. _For Davlatjon:_ Add one hidden 'gentle' flag to the 5 robots for age under 10 (and when the parent allows): after the child hangs a piece, the robot skips one obviously winning capture, and after 3 free good moves it plays one level stronger. Report it honestly to the parent ('Робот подстраивается'), and show it to the child as a line in the robot's voice ('Я немного поддался'), not as a number. Keep 'Турнир' mode non-adaptive and labelled that way.
- **Interactive micro-lesson: prompt, optional hint, a specific message for each wrong move, Next** (verified; https://lichess.org/blog/WtDErSQAADJfhJJs/interactive-lessons) — A Lichess interactive lesson shows a comment that describes the position and asks for the right move (default text 'What would you play in this position?'). A hidden hint appears only when the student clicks 'Get a hint', and if no hint is authored the button does not appear. Each specific wrong move can have its own authored error comment, and a general error message covers the rest. After a correct move, the lesson plays the reply and the student continues with Next or Space. _Why:_ One question per screen, feedback tied to the exact wrong move, and hints on demand are what the child-friendly part of the pattern is. This matches the owner's principles (soft feedback, hints one by one). I did not verify a study for the effect. _For Davlatjon:_ The Pawn exercise screen (kid7-phone-pawn-ex-t1.jpg) puts three tabs (Урок / Упражнения 0/7 / Словарик и факты), seven numbered chips, a section title, an instruction and the first question on one screen, and the board is below the fold. For Aziz, make a 'Lesson player' route: one question per full screen, the board and the question both visible, a lightbulb that reveals hints one by one, one 'Дальше' button, and a spoken prompt that auto-plays once. Author a per-wrong-move line for the 10 most common mistakes per level ('Пешка не ходит назад — смотри, куда она смотрит'), not one generic 'попробуй ещё'. Keep the three tabs for Dilnoza and for review.
- **Repeat-based training: tiny steps (Chessable) and repeated puzzle sets (Woodpecker), used honestly** (verified; https://notes.andymatuschak.org/zDr94hP6bG3jJYrdYy8B5hx and https://www.zwischenzug.gg/p/the-woodpecker-method-revisited) — Chessable's MoveTrainer, as described in Andy Matuschak's notes, works one move at a time: you read about a move, repeat it on the board, continue, and replay the whole sequence after a set. Answers are entered on the board, so grading is automatic. The same note lists limits: little narrative structure, and it tests moves rather than ideas. The Woodpecker method repeats a fixed puzzle set in faster cycles. The Zwischenzug article says its support is anecdotal (Tikkanen's GM norms, de la Maza's rating gains), that repetition may build memory of specific positions more than general patterns (it compares this to overfitting), and that its real value is that it keeps people practising. Both are designed for adults and strong players. _Why:_ Spacing and re-asking help a child remember a specific line. They do not prove that tactics skill transfers, and the Woodpecker claim is contested. _For Davlatjon:_ The app has a Woodpecker mode and spaced review. Keep them, but show them to the child as a game against their own last result ('В прошлый раз ты решил 5 за 4 минуты — попробуем снова?') and not as a clock. For age under 10, no timer: the goal is 'на этот раз без подсказок'. Mix new puzzles in every session so the child does not just memorise the answers. After a set, show one concept sentence ('Это называется вилка') to cover the ideas-not-moves gap.
- **Unrated friendly racing with no public leaderboard** (verified; https://lichess.org/blog/YFOLzhMAACIAarsp/new-feature-puzzle-racer) — Lichess Puzzle Racer is a competitive version of Puzzle Storm modelled on typeracer.com. Players join a lobby or share a custom link for groups of up to 10. It is unrated and does not affect puzzle rating, anonymous players get a random name, bots are not allowed, and it is free and ad-free. There is no leaderboard, because the team says leaderboards invite cheating and moderating them is not a good use of resources. _Why:_ Racing the same puzzles as a friend gives the social, competitive feeling Dilnoza wants with no rating at stake. The lack of a leaderboard here is a moderation decision. The page does not claim it is for child wellbeing. _For Davlatjon:_ Add 'Гонка с другом' on one device (the Play page already has 'вдвоём с мамой или папой на одном экране'): two players take turns on the same 5 puzzles (or both see the same set) with a 60-90 second round and a 'We both finished!' end screen with equal stars for finishing. Show 'твой лучший результат' and 'лучше, чем вчера', never a ranked list. For Dilnoza, the shareable result is a printable or screenshot card with the child's first name only and no surname or city.
- **Puzzle Storm mechanics, only for the older children and with a gentler penalty** (verified; https://lichess.org/blog/YBCoVBUAANCqHhLv/puzzlers-on-the-storm) — Puzzle Storm gives 3 minutes. Each correct puzzle is a point, each correct move fills a combo bar, a full bar gives a time bonus, and a wrong answer costs 10 seconds and resets the bar. When time runs out you see your score and the list of puzzles attempted, and you can open any of them. It has no leaderboard, shows your best daily and all-time scores on your profile, and is free with no ads. _Why:_ The variable time bonus keeps the clock from being predictable, and the end-of-round list turns a failed puzzle into something to study. Those are the stated design intents; there is no evidence in the page about children. _For Davlatjon:_ Davlatjon already has a storm. For age 10 and above keep the 3-minute round, but change the penalty: a wrong answer breaks the combo only (no -10 s), and the end screen shows 'Решено: N' and 'Лучшее: M', plus the tap-to-review list 'Разберём 2 задачи?'. For age under 9, hide Storm and offer 'Серия' (streak with no clock): 'Сколько подряд решишь?' with a visible, friendly reset.
- **Bite-sized mini-games with many short levels (without the lives)** (verified; https://apps.apple.com/np/app/magnus-trainer-train-chess/id1097863089) — The Magnus Trainer App Store listing describes '250+ unique lessons' and 'Bite-sized games designed to reinforce your learning', where each mini-game has dozens of levels and thousands of puzzles in total. The app is free, and members get 'infinite lives so you can always keep playing', and bonus levels and detailed statistics. The listing does not explain how lives work for free users, but it implies free play is limited by lives. _Why:_ One mini-game with many tiny levels gives a lot of 'one more' moments in 30-60 seconds. The lives are the monetisation, not the learning design. _For Davlatjon:_ The Drills page (rich-phone-drills-t1.jpg) is a good start: 'Пять минут в день', cards 'Кто в опасности?', 'Запомни', 'Конь', each with 'Рекорд: 4 из 6'. Make each drill a 10-level ladder with 1-minute levels and a visible 'Уровень 3 из 10' bar, and cap one session at about 5-7 minutes with a friendly 'На сегодня хватит — молодец' screen (Aziz's 10 minutes of attention). Keep unlimited retries with no lives and no loss counters.
- **A story world with earned cosmetics (ChessKid Adventure)** (verified; https://support.chesskid.com/en/articles/8887467-what-is-the-chesskid-adventure-app) — ChessKid Adventure was a fantasy-themed kids app with animated characters teaching the game, 40+ mythical characters to challenge across 15 levels, six quests, 200+ mini challenges, and gold coins used to collect costume outfits. The help page says the app is no longer supported. It does not say why, so I do not infer a reason. _Why:_ A map with a story gives a clear 'where am I going' to a child who cannot yet read a long list, and cosmetic rewards give a reason to come back with no performance pressure. I found no study of its effect. _For Davlatjon:_ The chess hub is 7.5 screens long with 48 interactive elements (metrics phone /chess; rich-phone-chess-t3.jpg shows a long vertical stack of cards: Дебюты, Знаменитые партии, Разбор партий, Эндшпиль). Add a 'Королевство' picture-map as the top of the hub for age under 10: 6 rank towers Пешка → Король, a lit path to the next lesson, and one big 'Продолжить' button. Move the history/encyclopedia/review/openings cards under a collapsed 'Ещё для любопытных' block. Let XP buy cosmetic robot outfits or board themes, never power.
- **A closed, adult-supervised social layer (no chat, auto-generated names, a guardian report)** (verified; https://www.chesskid.com/ and https://www.chesskid.com/learn/articles/how-to-understand-chesskids-safety-features2 and https://www.chesskid.com/learn/articles/chess-coaching-for-kids) — ChessKid's homepage lists 'no chat' and auto-generated usernames. Its safety article says kids cannot message or chat with each other, adults cannot talk to kids except a guardian or staff, friends are by request and acceptance, and guardians can turn off social access or read their kid's messages by impersonating the account. The homepage says parents receive activity reports and can approve screen time, and the coaching article lists reports, weekly goals by email, certificates and badges. The safety article does not describe a reporting tool. One ChessKid page says 'no chat' and another allows friend requests, so check the details before copying. _Why:_ Parents decide whether to let a child on a platform by the safety story first. Short reports let a busy parent see learning without opening the app. _For Davlatjon:_ Before Google/Telegram sync ships: no free-text fields that other people can read, no public profile, no friends list by default, the child's name stays on the device and in the parent view only. For the parent, one screen (behind the PIN) with 3 lines for the week: days played, what the child learned in a sentence ('Освоил вилку и ход коня'), and one suggested 5-minute activity to do together. Make the report a weekly share to the parent's Telegram, not a push at the child.
- **Touch targets and tap-or-drag for small hands** (verified; https://www.nngroup.com/articles/children-ux-physical-development/) — NN/g recommends 'at least 2cm × 2cm touch targets for young children', about four times the 1 cm size for adults, and reports a 5 mm close button that was too small for 7-year-olds. It says that under age 9, tapping, swiping and dragging work best, that precise dragging is hard even on touchscreens, that tasks should allow more than one way to complete (drag or tap), and that 7-9-year-olds did well with clear instructions with images. _Why:_ Accuracy and the fine-motor skill of a 7-year-old are lower than an adult's. Multiple input methods and forgiving targets prevent 'I did it right but it did not work' frustration. _For Davlatjon:_ My calculation, not a measurement: on a 6.3 inch Pixel 7 (412 CSS px wide) a board square is about 44 CSS px, which is about 7 mm, so the board cannot meet the 2 cm figure and the squares need a forgiving hit area. Make sure: (1) tap-tap and drag both work; (2) after the first tap, show large legal-move dots; (3) a drag snaps to the nearest legal square, not the exact one; (4) a lifted piece is drawn above the finger. Elsewhere, raise the controls under 44 px: /chess/play has 37 targets under 44 px, /chess/pawn 20, /chess/secrets 41 (audit-metrics.json); the 'Фора' chips are 32 px high and the colour buttons 36 px. Set a 48 px minimum for age under 10 in the app's token, not per page.
- **Wellbeing nudges: a calm end of session and 'pause and save'** (verified; https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/childrens-information/childrens-code-guidance-and-resources/age-appropriate-design-a-code-of-practice-for-online-services/13-nudge-techniques/) — The ICO's nudge-technique standard says designers must not use nudges to push children to give more data or lower privacy protection, and should not exploit unconscious psychological processes. It also says you may nudge children in ways that support health and wellbeing, such as taking breaks and 'mid-level pause and save features', and that younger children need instruction-based help and parental support. The page does not mention streaks, rewards or continuous play, so any application to streaks is my inference. _Why:_ A product that ends a session itself is the opposite of a design that keeps a child hooked. It is what a parent wants to see, and it protects Aziz's 10 minutes of attention. _For Davlatjon:_ After about 10 minutes of chess (6-8) or 20 (9-12), show one kind full-screen card: the robot waving, 'Хорошая игра! Партия сохранена. Продолжим завтра?' with a single 'Закончить' button and a smaller 'Ещё одну'. Auto-save every position so a game can be resumed. Keep the streak as 'gentle': no 'you lost your streak' message and no countdown; missing a day just shows 'С возвращением!'. Make the length a parent setting.
- **Honest claims to parents: skill, not 'makes you smarter'** (verified; https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/102237 (Sala & Gobet 2016 meta-analysis) and https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/102204 (Sala & Gobet 2017)) — The 2016 meta-analysis of 24 studies (40 effect sizes, 2,788 children in chess groups) found a moderate overall effect (g = 0.338), larger for maths (g = 0.382) than reading (g = 0.248), with a positive effect of treatment duration. The same authors' 2017 review of chess, music and working-memory training concludes the effects shrink as design quality improves (for example with active control groups) and that 'far transfer of learning rarely occurs'. The finding is contested: the 2016 paper reported a moderate effect and the later paper concludes far transfer is rare. _Why:_ Parents in Uzbekistan will ask 'does it help my child with maths?'. A claim you cannot support damages trust. _For Davlatjon:_ Keep the parent copy about observable chess and thinking habits ('научился замечать угрозы', 'стал решать без подсказок') and not about school grades. If you want a maths angle, say 'chess practice may help some children, and research is mixed', and show the child's real progress in the app's own math tasks next to the chess ones, since the platform has both.

Anti-patterns:

- Lives / hearts that stop a child from playing — The Magnus Trainer listing sells 'infinite lives' as a membership benefit, so free play is limited by lives (the listing does not explain the exact rule). For a 6-12-year-old, being locked out after a mistake teaches fear of mistakes and creates a friction a parent has to resolve. Davlatjon has no ads or paywalls and should keep unlimited retries.
- Rewards that shrink when a child asks for help — Chess.com awards 3 crowns for no help, 2 for 1-3 hints or undos, and 1 for 4 or more, applied to every user including kids. For a 7-year-old this can read as 'asking for help is bad', which works against hints and undo that the owner's principles want children to use. Give one crown per win and an optional bonus rim for no help.
- Time penalties and combo-loss visuals for children under 9 — Puzzle Storm takes 10 seconds and the combo bar for a wrong answer. It is built for adults and teens who want that pressure. For young children it teaches rushing and guessing, and stress on a small screen with 7 mm squares causes mis-taps that then feel like 'wrong' answers. Use no-clock streaks for under 9.
- Streak-loss guilt and loss-aversion nudges — From background knowledge, 'You'll lose your 12-day streak!' pushes a child to play out of anxiety, and one design-ethics article calls this the 'dark side' of streaks. The ICO nudge page does not mention streaks, but it does say not to exploit unconscious psychological processes and that wellbeing nudges (breaks, pause and save) are welcome. Keep the streak gentle: no loss message, no countdown, a 'С возвращением!' on return.
- Confirm-shaming and lopsided buttons — The ICO's own examples of nudge techniques include a large prominent 'yes' next to a small 'no', and framing one option's outcome more positively than the other. On a small screen with a child it is easy to build by accident (a big blue 'Играть' beside a tiny grey 'Не сейчас'). Make both choices the same size and wording neutral.
- Public leaderboards, free-text chat and custom avatars/usernames — ChessKid removes free chat, auto-generates usernames, and says it does not allow custom avatars (the support article cited in my search; I did not open that exact page). Lichess skipped leaderboards for Racer and Storm because they invite cheating and are costly to moderate. For Davlatjon's optional Google/Telegram sync, a visible name and a public rank would expose a child's identity and turn a learning tool into a contest; Dilnoza's wish to show friends is better met by a private card or printed certificate.
- Showing rating numbers, accuracy percentages and harsh move labels to children — From background knowledge, not verified: engine-style labels such as 'Blunder' or '62% accuracy' make a child feel judged by a machine. It contradicts the owner's soft-feedback and no-rating rules. Keep stars, 'нашёл лучший ход' and 'посмотрим вместе'; use the review page for the one interesting moment, not a list of errors.
- Reporting repetition speed as skill — The Woodpecker approach and spaced repetition can make a child faster on a set they have memorised, and the evidence for Woodpecker is anecdotal. A parent report that says 'solves 40% faster' would be misleading. Report 'solved without hints' and 'new puzzles solved' and not repeat speed.
- Marketing claims of intelligence or school-grade gains — The 2017 Sala and Gobet review concludes that far transfer rarely occurs, and the 2016 meta-analysis found effect sizes that depended on design quality. Telling Uzbek and Russian parents that chess raises grades sets an expectation the research does not back.

### Learning science and developmental psychology for a UI for children 6-12 (Davlatjon, Uzbekistan)

What survived checking: (1) Feedback quality and retrieval/spacing are the best-supported levers. Donoghue and Hattie 2021 (242 studies) report d=0.85 for distributed practice and 0.74 for practice testing, but mostly on surface, factual outcomes. (2) Praise and rewards need restraint. Deci, Koestner and Ryan 1999 (128 experiments) found tangible, expected rewards undermine free-choice interest, harder on children than on college students, while positive informational feedback raised interest (d about 0.31-0.33). (3) Growth mindset is heavily contested. Macnamara and Burgoyne 2023 find d=0.05, non-significant after bias correction and in the 6 best studies. Yeager 2019 (n=12,490) found d=0.11 only for lower-achieving students, and only where school peer norms supported it. So use process-specific feedback because the feedback literature supports it, not as a mindset cure. (4) Productive failure is NOT a default for young children. Sinha and Kapur 2021 (53 studies) report g=0.36 overall, but for grades 2-5 instruction-first did better. That fits Aziz (7) and argues for worked example then try, with struggle-first only for Dilnoza-type learners in short bursts. (5) Kids behave like adults on usability. NN/g found that children skip long instructions, avoid scrolling, can't tell ads from content, and need separate designs for 6-8 and 9-12. (6) Streaks work, but even Duolingo's own blog concedes that fear of losing a streak can stop people starting one, and its freeze feature gave only +0.38% daily actives. A gentle streak is the right call and Davlatjon already has one. (7) Things I could not verify and the owner should not treat as fact: any "age + N minutes" attention-span rule (no traceable primary source; sources say it applies to uninteresting tasks), Mayer's modality/redundancy results in pre-readers (the principles come mostly from adult studies, so extrapolating to Aziz is a reasoned hypothesis), and the exact Piaget age bands (background knowledge, and the stages are criticised). Net advice for Davlatjon: keep its existing principles (soft feedback, one-by-one hints, no ratings for under-10s, recorded voice). Shorten the unit of play for 6-8. Make audio the primary channel for the youngest. Turn feedback into process statements. Keep rewards informational and predictable. Add spaced retrieval to the daily quest. Give Dilnoza visible mastery and a shareable proof without public ranking. App evidence from the audit: kid7 home promises "8 задач · около 25 минут" for one day (kid7-phone-home-t1.jpg), against a roughly 10-minute attention budget for Aziz. The day-1 task shows "Прочитать" as a small text chip beside the counter (kid7-phone-day1-t1-t1.jpg). /chess/pawn on a phone has 20 targets under 44 px and 11 under 32 px; /chess/history has 120 under 32 px and 402 text nodes under 14 px (audit-metrics.json). The "Режим занятий: 6-8 лет · изменить" line is a good adaptive-by-age idea but is tiny.

- **1. Autonomy through bounded choice (SDT)** (unverified; background knowledge (Ryan and Deci 2000, Self-Determination Theory; the selfdeterminationtheory.org page I opened lists only citations)) — SDT holds that motivation lasts when three needs are met: autonomy (I choose), competence (I can), relatedness (I matter to someone). Autonomy support means offering real choices and rationale and avoiding pressure and controlling language. Vansteenkiste's classroom experiments (reported in search summaries, not opened) found that inviting framing led to deeper processing and more persistence than pressuring framing. _Why:_ Choice makes the activity the child's own, so engagement does not depend on outside pressure. Controlling wording ('you must', 'don't break your streak') shifts motivation from interest to obligation. _For Davlatjon:_ On the home hero (kid7-phone-home-t1.jpg) the child gets one orange Начать. Keep that single path as the default, and add a visible low-friction choice: 'Today pick 1 of 3' (a math tool, a chess puzzle, a story) with big icon cards, and let the daily quest be satisfiable in any order. Rephrase quest and award copy from commands ('Реши 3 задачи') to invitations ('Хочешь попробовать 3 задачи?'). Let the child pick the avatar and the robot opponent's name. Keep the Russian gender-neutral rule when rephrasing.
- **2. Competence made visible as 'what I can do now', not as a score** (unverified; background knowledge (SDT competence need; Sailer and Homner 2020 gamification meta-analysis found small positive effects, g=.49 cognitive, .36 motivational, .25 behavioural, from search summary, not opened)) — A progress display framed around skills gained: a skill map where each node says 'I can ...' (balance scales, knight forks), with a short 'before / after' example. Rank titles (Pawn to King) already do some of this. _Why:_ Competence feedback tied to concrete mastery is informational, not controlling. Deci et al. 1999 (opened via Europe PMC) found positive feedback raised free-choice interest (d about 0.33) and self-reported interest (d about 0.31). Gamification meta-analysis effects are small and less stable for motivation under strict methodological checks (search summary). _For Davlatjon:_ Replace or complement raw XP and 'упражнений решено 0 из 43' (kid7-phone-chess-t1.jpg) with a sticker/skill board: each exercise group unlocks a named 'I can' card ('Я умею ставить мат ладьёй'). For Dilnoza add a progress timeline that can be exported as the existing printable certificate. For the parent, the same data reads as a sentence ('Ана освоила 6 приёмов на этой неделе'). Never show the hidden puzzle rating to under-10s, as the owner already decided.
- **3. Relatedness without public ranking: co-play, show-a-grown-up, shareable proof** (unverified; background knowledge (SDT relatedness need; Sailer and Homner 2020 reported collaboration combined with competition as the more effective combination, from search summary, not opened)) — Features that connect the child to a trusted person: a 'show this to mum/dad' end-of-session screen, a printable certificate (already built), a family challenge, and a friendly guide character that speaks to the child. _Why:_ Relatedness is the third SDT need, and for 6-12 the people who matter are parents, siblings, a teacher and 1-3 close friends, not a global leaderboard. _For Davlatjon:_ Add a 'Покажи маме/папе' (UZ equivalent) button after a session that opens one clean card with today's win and a one-line prompt for the parent ('Спросите: как ты нашёл этот путь?'). Dilnoza gets a link or image export of a certificate or a puzzle result. Optionally a private 'duel the same puzzle' between two named friends via a code, with no global ranks. Connect to the existing /parent area through a daily one-line summary.
- **4. Challenge-skill balance with a quiet 'comfortable' dial (flow)** (unverified; background knowledge (Csikszentmihalyi's flow; Donoghue and Hattie 2021 effect-size context opened)) — Keep the task slightly above current skill with clear goals and immediate feedback. Davlatjon already tags tasks with 'Комфортно' (kid7-phone-day1-t1-t1.jpg) and has a hidden puzzle rating. _Why:_ Too easy bores and too hard produces anxiety. Flow is a useful design heuristic, but its strong causal claims about learning are mostly correlational (background knowledge). _For Davlatjon:_ Make the difficulty tag a child-controlled soft dial: after 2 smooth wins offer 'Хочется сложнее?', after 2 stuck attempts offer 'Давай чуть проще' as a friendly choice, never an automatic silent downgrade. Give each puzzle a clear one-sentence goal at the top ('Поставь мат в 1 ход'). Keep the rating hidden from under-10s. For Dilnoza show a '3 levels of challenge' selector on the puzzle hub.
- **5. Scaffolding in the ZPD, with worked example first for the youngest** (verified; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.3102/00346543211019105 (Sinha and Kapur 2021, Review of Educational Research, metadata and abstract summary I opened)) — Vygotsky's zone of proximal development (background knowledge): learners can do more with support than alone, and support should fade. Productive failure (Kapur) lets learners attempt a problem before being taught. Sinha and Kapur's meta-analysis of 53 studies (166 comparisons) found problem-solving-first beat instruction-first overall (g=0.36), and more when it followed PF principles (g 0.37-0.58), but for grades 2-5 and domain-general skills instruction-first did better. _Why:_ Novices lack the prior knowledge to benefit from open struggle. The tool-based tasks (robot programmer, balance scales) are guided exploration, so the question is when to show the example. _For Davlatjon:_ For ages 6-8 run 'watch one worked example (animated, voiced) then try a twin problem'. Keep hints opening one by one, ending with an optional 'show me' replay. For Dilnoza-level kids (10+) offer an optional 'try first, then see the idea' mode on a puzzle theme, then show the solution idea. Fade scaffolds as the child succeeds: first hint appears after 20 s, then only on request.
- **6. Specific process feedback instead of 'you are smart' (with mindset replication caveat)** (verified; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36326645/ via Europe PMC record (Macnamara and Burgoyne 2023, Psychological Bulletin) and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786290/ (Yeager et al. 2019, Nature); Mueller and Dweck 1998 via https://www.progressfocused.com/2020/09/mueller-dweck-1998-classic-study.html (secondary summary)) — Mueller and Dweck (1998, fifth graders) found intelligence praise ('you must be smart') led to more easy-task choices, worse post-failure performance and lower enjoyment than effort praise. The wider growth-mindset claim is contested. Yeager 2019: 12,490 ninth graders, two sessions of about 25 minutes, +0.10 GPA (standardised 0.11) for lower-achieving students only, larger where peer norms were supportive. Macnamara and Burgoyne 2023: 63 studies, N=97,672, overall d=0.05, non-significant after bias correction, 0.04 where mindset actually shifted, 0.02 in the 6 best studies. Burnette et al. 2023 reported d=0.14 for academics with targeted, high-fidelity samples (search summary only). _Why:_ The defensible core is narrow: praise should describe what the child did (strategy, effort, a check she made), which also matches Hattie and Timperley's process level. Treat 'growth mindset lessons' as unproven. _For Davlatjon:_ Audit every success string and replace identity praise ('Умница!', 'Гений!') with process statements that are true and specific: 'Ты проверил каждый ход перед шагом, поэтому нашёл мат', 'Ты нашёл другой путь'. Keep soft feedback after misses ('Почти! Давай посмотрим ещё раз'). Do not add mindset lectures or posters. Use neutral wording in Russian so no gendered adjective is needed, matching the owner's rule.
- **7. Informational, predictable rewards (avoid over-justification)** (verified; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:10589297&resultType=core&format=json (Deci, Koestner and Ryan 1999, Psychological Bulletin; record I opened)) — Meta-analysis of 128 experiments: engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent rewards all reduced later free-choice interest (d -0.40, -0.36, -0.28); tangible and expected rewards reduced it; engagement- and completion-contingent rewards also reduced self-reported interest. Positive feedback increased interest (d about 0.31-0.33). Tangible rewards were more harmful for children than for college students, and verbal rewards less beneficial for children. Cameron and Pierce (1994) and later critics dispute the size of the undermining effect, so it is contested but consistent with the SDT view. _Why:_ A reward that signals 'you did this for the prize' turns play into a job. Information about skill ('you solved it without a hint') keeps the activity the child's own. _For Davlatjon:_ Keep XP, levels, crowns and certificates as informational markers of mastery, not as payment. Do not attach tangible or purchasable prizes to playing. Do not advertise the reward before the task ('Solve 3 to get 50 XP!'), since expected rewards are the harmful kind. Show the earned marker afterward. Make the daily quest ('3 things') a suggestion, not a debt. In parent copy say 'we reward understanding, not time spent'.
- **8. Low cognitive load, audio-first for pre-readers, text for fluent readers** (unverified; background knowledge (Sweller's cognitive load theory; Mayer's multimedia principles; Kalyuga's expertise-reversal effect); child-specific evidence was thin in my searches) — Working memory is small (about 3-4 chunks in adults per Cowan, and children have less capacity per search summaries) so extraneous load should be removed: one task per screen, words next to the image they describe, no decorative motion. Mayer's modality principle says narration plus picture beats picture plus on-screen text. The redundancy principle says narration plus identical on-screen text can hurt fluent readers. Expertise reversal says what helps novices can hinder experts. _Why:_ Aziz spends most working memory decoding words, leaving little for the maths. Dilnoza decodes automatically and can scan text faster than listen. Executive-function limits (planning, inhibition) mean kids also benefit from visible goals and 'where am I' cues. _For Davlatjon:_ For under-8s: make the speaker the primary control on every task and lesson, as a big icon-only button (44-56 px) at the top of the card, and auto-play the narration once on first view (with a mute toggle), instead of the small text chip 'Прочитать' seen in kid7-phone-day1-t1-t1.jpg. Highlight the word being spoken (background knowledge, not tested here for Uzbek). Cap task text at about 2 short lines plus a picture. For Dilnoza keep text-first with audio optional. Add a persistent goal strip ('Цель: собрать 3 звезды') and a step indicator for multi-step tools such as the robot programmer. Add Undo to all board and tool actions.
- **9. Retrieval practice and spaced return built into the daily quest** (verified; https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2021.581216/full (Donoghue and Hattie 2021) and Cepeda et al. 2008 via Europe PMC record (PMID 19076480)) — Donoghue and Hattie meta-analysed the 10 Dunlosky techniques (242 studies, 169,179 participants, mean g 0.56): distributed practice d=0.85, practice testing d=0.74. Effects were larger for lower- than for higher-ability students, mostly on surface outcomes (0.60 vs 0.26 for deep) and short delays, and primary students showed lower effects for some techniques. Cepeda 2008 (1,350+ adults) found the optimal gap grows with the retention interval, from about 20-40% of a 1-week delay to about 5-10% of a 1-year delay. _Why:_ Pulling an idea out of memory after a gap strengthens it more than re-reading. Feedback after the attempt matters ('extremely robust' in the Frontiers paper). _For Davlatjon:_ Make the existing spaced-review feature a first-class daily-quest item: a 2-minute 'Вспомни' set of 3 items from 1, 3 and 7 days ago, with a retry that is framed as a game ('верни пропавшую звезду'). Use the child's own earlier errors (the 'Мои задачи' page). Show the parent a line: 'повторили то, что учили 3 дня назад'. Keep recall questions low-stakes, with no timer for Aziz.
- **10. Feedback that answers 'where am I going, how am I doing, what next'** (unverified; background knowledge, with the abstract and four-level model seen via search summaries (Hattie and Timperley 2007, Review of Educational Research 77(1), 81-112); I did not open the paper) — The model distinguishes feedback about the task, the process, self-regulation and the self (praise). Summaries say task, process and self-regulation levels help most and self-level praise helps least. Novices need task and process cues, more proficient learners benefit from self-regulation prompts. I could not confirm the 0.79 effect-size figure that is often quoted. _Why:_ Good feedback closes the gap between the current state and the goal and says what to do next. Pure approval carries no information. _For Davlatjon:_ Standardise every response into three parts: what happened (task: 'ладья осталась без защиты'), a pointer to the idea (process: 'проверь, кто может её съесть'), and a next step (a 'Ещё раз' button and a 'Подсказка' button). Keep the 'no wrong' rule and call it 'пока не получилось'. For Dilnoza add a self-check habit prompt ('Что проверишь до хода?') after the second miss. For puzzle failure in chess show the refutation on the board, not as text.
- **11.
